Where it began

Phil Tufnell was born in Barnet on 29 April 1966. He went to Highgate School, where his cricket was good enough for him to captain the junior first XI before he reached the top year, and then to Southgate School. By one account he was opening both the batting and the bowling for his club's juniors at the age of nine, which, given what came later, makes the first of those a remarkable claim.

He joined Middlesex in 1986 and stayed with them until 2002.

The player

Tufnell bowled slow left-arm orthodox spin, and between 1990 and 2001 he won 42 Test caps and played 20 one-day internationals. He took 121 Test wickets at 37.69, with five five-wicket innings, two ten-wicket matches and a best of 7 for 47. He was in the squad that reached the final of the 1992 World Cup.

Two days at the Oval stand out. In 1991 he took 6 for 25 against West Indies, and in 1997 he took eleven wickets for 93 runs against Australia to win the match by 19 runs and the Man of the Match award. In all first-class cricket he took 1,057 wickets.

What made him special

When the conditions suited him he could spin a side out, and the best batsmen knew it. Mark Waugh, who thought the trick was to attack him, fell to him seven times in Tests, more than anyone else.

Batting was another matter. Tufnell was the classic number 11, nervous and a little awkward at the crease. He made 153 Test runs at 5.10 with a best of 22 not out, though it should be said that he was not out in 29 of his 59 innings, so bowlers did not find him quite as easy to remove as the average suggests. His fielding, once a worry, improved as his career went on.

Away from the middle

He was nicknamed The Cat, for his gift for falling asleep in a corner of the dressing room, and Two Sugars, for his love of tea. After cricket his cheerful nature made him a broadcaster and a television favourite. He won I'm a Celebrity in 2003, was a team captain on They Think It's All Over and A Question of Sport, danced on Strictly Come Dancing in 2009, and became a summariser on Test Match Special in 2003. Middlesex University gave him an honorary doctorate in 2011, and for years he served as president of the cricket charity The Change Foundation.

And finally

Plenty of cricketers end up on the radio. Few arrive there having been named after a sleeping cat and a cup of tea, which may be why listeners always felt they could put the kettle on and settle in with him.
